lesson.profit_loss.hook: Asha buys 50 samosas for {buy} and sells them all for {sell}. Did she do well?
lesson.profit_loss.define: **Profit** is what you have left after paying your costs. If you end up with less, that is a **loss**. **Return** is the profit as a percentage of what you put in. It lets you compare small and big amounts.
lesson.profit_loss.paper: A gain or loss on something you still hold is a **paper** gain or loss. It becomes **realised** only when you sell.
lesson.profit_loss.analogy: Think of a tea stall. You spend {buy} on milk, tea and sugar. Customers pay {sell}. The extra money is your profit. Return tells you how hard each rupee worked.
lesson.profit_loss.worked: Asha's profit is {profit1}. Her return is {ret1}: that is {profit1} earned on {buy} put in. On a bad day she sells for {lowSell}. That is a loss of {lossAbs}, and a return of {ret2}.
lesson.profit_loss.predict.q: Your {startAmt} falls by {fall}. What rise brings it back to {startAmt}?
lesson.profit_loss.predict.explain: It needs a rise of {needGain}, not {fall}. After the fall you hold {afterFall}. To get back to {startAmt}, that {afterFall} must double.
lesson.profit_loss.tradeoff: A big percentage on a small amount can be fewer rupees than a small percentage on a big amount. A gain of {smallPct} on {smallBase} is {smallGain}. A gain of {bigPct} on {bigBase} is {bigGain}. Always look at both the rupees and the percentage.
lesson.profit_loss.mistake: Many people think a fall of {fall} and a rise of {fall} cancel out. They do not. {startAmt} falls to {afterFall}, then rises to only {afterRise}.
lesson.profit_loss.formula: Return = (value now - value you paid) ÷ value you paid. To recover from a fall of x, you need a rise of x ÷ (1 - x).
